When the evidence is part of the Definition of Done, it exists the day the item closes.

Every automotive quality manager knows the four weeks before an ASPICE assessment or a functional safety audit. Engineers stop engineering and start reconstructing: trace matrices rebuilt in spreadsheets, review records written for reviews that happened months ago, verification reports assembled from whatever the test bench logged. Teams that adopted sprints often find this scramble got worse, because the sprints moved fast and the evidence never kept up.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. This post is written for safety and quality managers, and for the systems engineers who answer to them. It covers what Automotive SPICE and ISO 26262 actually permit for agile teams, where those teams really fall short, and how to produce the evidence inside the sprint so the scramble stops being necessary. It completes a short series with how to run the V-model and agile sprints at the same time and six hybrid workflows compared, and draws on my field guide, Sprinting through the V.

What the Standards Actually Say​

The scepticism deserves to be taken seriously first. Both standards exist because informal development produced unsafe and unmaintainable systems, and "we're agile now" has been used to justify skipping work that matters. A safety manager who hears that phrase and reaches for the standard is doing the job well.

The standards themselves, though, are clearer than most of the debate around them.

Automotive SPICE assesses whether process outcomes are achieved and whether the evidence for them exists. It defines processes, base practices and work products, and leaves the lifecycle to the organisation. intacs, the body that certifies ASPICE assessors, publishes Agile SPICE, an assessment model aligned with Automotive SPICE 4.0 that adds three agile processes: AGL.1 Agile Work Management, AGL.2 Partner Collaboration Management and AGL.3 Agile Quality Assurance. It maps everyday agile practice onto ASPICE base practices and work products, which gives an assessor a recognised way to read an agile project.

ISO 26262 addresses agile directly, which surprises many people. In Part 6, clause 5.2, NOTE 1 states that development approaches from agile software development can be suitable for safety-related software, provided any tailoring of the safety activities follows ISO 26262-2:2018 clause 6.4.5. The same note sets the limit plainly: agile approaches "cannot be used to omit safety measures", nor to ignore the documentation, process or product rigour that functional safety requires. The examples that follow in the same clause name test-driven development and continuous integration on an automated build system, including documentation generation and testing.

Two precise points matter here. That note sits in Part 6, which covers the software level. At system and hardware level, the route is the general tailoring provision in Part 2, with the rationale recorded in the safety plan. And the note is informative guidance attached to normative requirements that do not change. Agile buys you freedom in how the work is sequenced. It buys no reduction in rigour.

Where Agile Teams Actually Fall Short​

If agile is permitted, why do agile teams so often struggle in assessments? The best evidence comes from a mapping study presented at ICSSP 2017, How do agile practices support Automotive SPICE compliance? by Diebold, Zehler and Richter. Mapping agile practices against ASPICE requirements, they found supporting practices for around 96% of base practices and around 87% of work products.

That is a mapping on paper, and an assessment rating would be stricter, so the exact numbers matter less than their shape. Agile teams already do the activities. What they under-produce is the artefacts. In practice that shows up as the familiar findings: bidirectional traceability missing or reconstructed late, work products created after the fact, and requirements that exist in the requirements tool, in the ticket system and in a specification document, each saying something slightly different.

That diagnosis is useful, because it tells you where to invest. Agile teams need help with evidence far more than with process.

Put the Evidence in the Definition of Done​

The single mechanism that closes the gap is the Definition of Done. If it names the trace links, the review record and the verification result, the evidence exists the moment an item closes. If it doesn't, the evidence gets produced weeks before the assessment by people reconstructing intent they no longer remember, at several times the cost.

A Definition of Done that carries compliance evidence looks like this for every item:

  • Model changes merged and consistency checks passing
  • Trace links complete: upward to the parent requirement, downward to the realisation, across to verification
  • Verification artefact present, with its result recorded
  • Peer review of the change recorded
  • Generated work products regenerated and current
  • No new orphan or unallocated elements introduced

Safety-relevant items carry additional criteria:

  • ASIL attribute set on every affected model element
  • Trace to the functional safety requirement and the safety goal
  • Verification method appropriate to the ASIL
  • Safety manager review recorded
  • Impact on safety analyses (FMEA, FTA, dependent failure analysis) assessed, with follow-up items raised where needed
  • Safety case claim updated with the new evidence

The test of whether this is working is simple. If the team ever schedules a "documentation sprint" to catch up on evidence from earlier sprints, the Definition of Done is not being enforced. The right response is to fix the Definition of Done and never to schedule the sprint, because once the catch-up sprint exists, every later sprint will rely on it.

Generate Work Products From the Model​

A Definition of Done like the one above is only achievable if producing the evidence is cheap. If closing an item means writing three documents, it will not happen inside a two-week sprint, and nobody should pretend otherwise.

The way through is to stop authoring work products and start generating them. When requirements, architecture, interfaces, allocation and verification live in a SysML model, the system requirements specification, the traceability matrix, the interface specification, the architecture description and the verification report become views of that model. A generated document is consistent with the model by construction, which removes an entire category of assessment finding: the one where two artefacts describe the same thing differently. Running a report fits inside a sprint in a way that writing a document never will. ISO 26262-6 itself lists documentation generation as part of the continuous integration example quoted above.

There is a cost here that many write-ups skip. If a generator, a model checker or a CI pipeline produces or checks safety-relevant work products, ISO 26262-8 requires confidence in that software tool. The tool is classified by its potential impact and by how likely its errors are to be detected, and the resulting tool confidence level determines whether qualification is needed. Plan for that once per toolchain configuration. It is a one-off investment, and a qualified, validated generator is precisely what makes generated evidence trustworthy to an assessor.

Configuration management carries the same weight in both standards. Baseline the model at every sprint boundary, so each review demonstrates against a named, immutable snapshot, and keep external deliveries on separate, less frequent baselines so nobody confuses what the team has explored with what the programme has formally committed.

Treat Safety Requirements as Backlog Items​

Some safety work genuinely belongs at the front, and a hybrid that pretends otherwise loses the safety manager's trust immediately. The item definition, the hazard analysis and risk assessment, and the functional safety concept belong in sprint zero and the first programme increment. Expect to revise them; a revised HARA is far cheaper than a missing one. What you buy by front-loading them is a stable boundary. Once the safety goals and the safety architecture exist, iteration inside them is low-risk, and any change that would cross them becomes visible instead of silent.

Inside that boundary, technical safety requirements, safety mechanisms and their verification become backlog items like any other, held to the stricter Definition of Done above. Agile SPICE's AGL.3 fits naturally here: safety review findings are tracked independently of the team's own backlog priorities, so they cannot be quietly ranked below feature work.

The safety case changes character too. In a sequential programme it is assembled at the end, often by whoever is available, from whatever was recorded. In this workflow the argument structure is drafted early, during the functional safety concept, and every sprint that completes a safety-relevant item attaches its verification evidence to the relevant claim. The safety case grows steadily, and at any moment you can see exactly which claims are still unsupported. That visibility is most of the benefit.

What Stays Independent and Event-Based​

One distinction matters a great deal, and agile writing often blurs it. The safety manager's review inside the Definition of Done is a verification activity within the team's flow. ISO 26262's confirmation measures are a different thing: the confirmation reviews, the functional safety audit and the functional safety assessment. They require a degree of independence, from I0 to I3, that rises with ASIL and is set out in the standard's tables, and they are planned in the safety plan.

A team cannot self-organise its way around an independent assessment. Confirmation measures stay event-based, scheduled at programme-increment boundaries against formal baselines, and an ASPICE assessment remains an event too. What changes is what those events find. When evidence has been produced and reviewed continuously, an assessment confirms a known state of the work, and it stops being a hunt for defects that nobody knew were there.

Measure the Evidence, Not the Documents​

The most useful leading indicator is evidence completeness: the percentage of completed backlog items whose trace links and verification artefacts are actually present. Track it every sprint, aiming for 100%. It predicts assessment outcomes many months ahead, which is exactly when there is still time to act on it.

Alongside it, trace health, meaning the count of orphan requirements, unallocated functions and requirements without verification, should come straight out of automated model checks and trend towards zero within each programme increment. The metric to retire is percentage-complete on documents. A specification that is 90% written says nothing about whether the system will work or the evidence will hold.

Where to Start​

Pick one pilot subsystem with real content and moderate safety relevance. ASIL A or B is ideal, since QM teaches you little and ASIL D is a hard place to learn. Write the Definition of Done with the evidence requirements explicit, automate the trace and consistency checks, and enforce the Definition of Done strictly from the first sprint. The first time an item is rejected because a trace link is missing is the moment the approach becomes real. Generate the first work products from the model early and show them to your quality department, or to a friendly assessor, while there is still time to adjust. Adopt Agile SPICE as the interpretation layer before your next assessment, so the assessor's first question, which lifecycle is this and how does it satisfy the model, already has a defensible answer.

The full ninety-day adoption sequence, the complete Definition of Ready and Done checklists including the hardware additions, and a twelve-week worked example on an EV traction inverter are in the book.

From MBSE Explained

Sprinting through the V

A 43-page field guide to running automotive V-model programmes on real agile sprints — with ASPICE and ISO 26262 evidence produced as you go, not reconstructed before the audit.

Read more about the book →

items.title: Agile ASPICE and ISO 26262: Compliance Evidence Inside the Sprint
items.summary: Can an agile team pass ASPICE and ISO 26262? Yes, if evidence lives in the Definition of Done. What the standards allow, and how to build it in the sprint.

items.content_html:
Six ways automotive teams combine the V-model with agile, and what each one actually covers.

Search for "V-model vs agile" and the same comparison table appears everywhere: sequential against iterative, documentation against working software, predictability against flexibility. For a web application that framing is useful. For an automotive programme under Automotive SPICE and ISO 26262 it misses the point, because the programme does not get to choose. The customer, the assessor and the safety case need the V's evidence structure, and the engineers need short feedback loops, so every real team ends up running some combination of the two.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. Several such combinations already exist, at different levels of formality, and your organisation is probably running one of them already, possibly by accident. This post compares six, says plainly what each gets right and where it stops, and ends with a way to choose. It draws on Part II of my field guide, Sprinting through the V.

Both Sides, Fairly​

The V-model's strengths are real. Bidirectional traceability links every requirement to its realisation and verification. Each specification level has a corresponding test level. Level discipline keeps the record navigable. Automotive also has genuine sequential forces behind it, from hardware lead times measured in weeks per spin, to supplier contracts signed against frozen baselines, to certification events that are expensive to repeat.

Agile's strengths are just as real, and they come down to feedback latency. A strictly sequential V can leave six to twelve months between an architectural decision and the integration result that tells you whether it was right. Incremental delivery, planning from observation and short feedback loops all exist to shrink that interval while decisions are still cheap to change.

The two operate on different layers. The V describes what evidence must exist and how it connects, and the sprint describes when work is planned and inspected. Once that is clear, "versus" stops being the question, and the practical question becomes which combination to run. The method itself is covered in How to Run the V-Model and Agile Sprints at the Same Time; this post is about the landscape.

1. Water-Scrum-Fall, the Accidental Default​

Requirements and architecture happen up front, implementation happens in sprints, and integration and verification happen at the end, so Scrum occupies the middle third of the lifecycle. Nobody chooses this. It is what an organisation gets when it introduces Scrum to its development teams and changes nothing about how requirements arrive or how releases are governed.

It works when requirements are stable and the software is a well-understood re-application of an existing platform, such as a facelift reusing most of a proven inverter software stack. Everywhere else it fails in two ways. Architectural feedback still arrives at integration, and verification is still a phase, which makes it the phase that absorbs schedule pressure. If your sprint reviews have no executable content and your requirements were written by another group before sprint one, this is what you are running.

2. The Agile-V Hybrid​

This is a family of practitioner models that keep the V as the overall lifecycle and traceability structure while executing each phase iteratively. Sprints become the execution mechanism and gates remain the commitment mechanism. Its appeal is low adoption cost. There is no reorganisation, no new set of role names, and the artefacts are the ones assessors and customers already recognise.

Its weakness is that it is under-specified. "Run each phase iteratively" leaves the hard questions open. How do you slice a system architecture into sprint-sized items, what does Done mean for an architecture increment, and what happens when a sprint invalidates an earlier baseline? Left unanswered, teams drift back to Water-Scrum-Fall. It is the right starting frame, and insufficient on its own.

3. SAFe​

The Scaled Agile Framework organises multiple teams into an Agile Release Train of roughly 50 to 125 people, planning together in Program Increments that typically run eight to twelve weeks, with a large cross-team planning event at the start of each. Automotive adopted it because it solves something team-level Scrum never touches, which is dependency management at the scale of a vehicle programme. The increment boundary maps naturally onto sample builds and milestone deliveries.

The cost is weight. SAFe brings a substantial vocabulary and role structure, so adopting it is an organisational change programme in its own right, and it says little about engineering itself: how to decompose an architecture, maintain traceability, or produce safety evidence. Teams sometimes adopt SAFe and find their ASPICE findings unchanged, because SAFe never addressed them. It is excellent at the programme layer for large programmes. With three teams it is overkill, and with fifteen you will end up building something like it anyway.

4. Agile SPICE​

Agile SPICE is published by intacs, the body that certifies Automotive SPICE assessors, as a process reference and assessment model designed to work alongside ASPICE. It adds three agile processes, AGL.1 Agile Work Management, AGL.2 Partner Collaboration Management and AGL.3 Agile Quality Assurance, and maps everyday agile practices such as sprints, backlogs and retrospectives onto ASPICE base practices and work products. It is aligned with Automotive SPICE 4.0.

Its biggest contribution is political. It dismantles the belief, held sincerely at many Tier 1s, that agile and ASPICE are incompatible, and it comes from the same community that trains assessors, which gives it credibility in exactly the room where credibility matters. AGL.2 also covers something no general agile framework does, the OEM to Tier 1 to Tier 2 supply chain. Its limit is that it is an assessment model. It describes what good looks like when assessed and leaves you to work out how to run a Tuesday. Adopt it as the compliance layer, whatever execution workflow sits underneath. How to produce the evidence it expects inside the sprint is covered in agile ASPICE and ISO 26262.

5. Harmony aMBSE​

Bruce Powel Douglass's agile model-based systems engineering process is the most engineering-specific of the six. Its defining idea is three nested cadences. A nanocycle of thirty minutes to a day verifies every model change immediately, ideally by executing it. A microcycle runs one to four weeks, and a macrocycle spans the project. It rejects big design up front in favour of developing and verifying the design work needed now.

It is the only one of the six that operates at the granularity engineers actually work at, and the only one that treats executable models as the verification mechanism. If your SysML model can be simulated, verification stops being a downstream phase. The catch is that it assumes mature modelling and tooling that supports execution, which is a large assumption in an organisation still arguing about whether the architecture lives in Cameo or in PowerPoint. It is also quiet on the commercial side of automotive, meaning supplier interfaces, sample milestones and customer change management.

6. The W-Model​

The W-model is less a workflow than a change to the V's shape. It runs test activities in parallel with each development activity, so test planning and test case design happen alongside the specification they verify. Writing system qualification test cases at the same time as the system requirements exposes an unverifiable requirement the moment someone tries to test it.

It is the cheapest meaningful improvement available to a sequential organisation, because it changes when an activity happens without changing who does it. It does nothing for planning, prioritisation or change management, so it shortens one feedback loop and leaves the others alone. Every hybrid should absorb it, ideally as a Definition of Done rule.

Side by Side​

Water-Scrum-FallAgile-V hybridSAFeAgile SPICEHarmony aMBSEW-model
Primary layerTeamProgramme + teamPortfolio + programmeAssessmentTeam + engineeringVerification
Multi-team scalingNoWeaklyYes, its main purposePartly (AGL.2)NoNo
Engineering methodNoPartlyNoNoYesPartly
ASPICE evidenceNoNoNoYes, its main purposePartlyNo
Needs MBSE maturityNoNoNoNoYesNo
Adoption costZeroLowVery highLow to mediumMediumVery low
Typical failureCeremony without feedbackDrift back to sequentialOverhead exceeds benefitCompliance without agilityStalls on tooling gapsSolves too little

Reading down the columns, a pattern appears. No single framework covers the whole problem, and the gaps are complementary. SAFe owns multi-team coordination, Harmony owns the engineering method, Agile SPICE owns the evidence layer, the W-model owns verification timing, and the Agile-V hybrid supplies the overall frame.

Which One Should You Pick?​

If you would rather pick one than assemble your own, two variables decide most of it: how many teams you have, and how mature your modelling is.

  • One to three teams with strong modelling: Harmony aMBSE plus the W-model verification rule, adding Agile SPICE once an assessment is scheduled.
  • One to three teams with weak modelling: the Agile-V hybrid plus the W-model rule, investing the difference in building the model backbone. Skip SAFe entirely.
  • Four to ten teams: the Agile-V hybrid with a programme-increment layer for cross-team planning. SAFe's PI planning event is worth borrowing on its own, without the rest of the framework.
  • More than ten teams across sites: SAFe, with an explicit engineering method underneath, because SAFe will not supply one.
  • An assessment within twelve months: Agile SPICE first and the workflow second, because the assessment will not wait for your transformation.

The Variable That Matters More Than the Framework​

One factor predicts success better than any choice in that table, and it is whether the organisation is willing to change its gate criteria.

If gates still demand complete artefacts across full scope, every one of these workflows degrades into Water-Scrum-Fall within two or three programmes, because the documentation push before each gate consumes whatever slack the sprints created. If gates are redefined around committed scope, with the remainder explicitly deferred and tracked, almost any of them produces an improvement. That change sits with programme management and quality. It is why so many agile transformations in automotive stall even when the engineering teams do their part.

Building a Composite Workflow​

Because the gaps are complementary, the workflow in Sprinting through the V is a composite. It takes the three-cadence structure from Harmony, the milestone-facing programme increment and its planning event from SAFe without the rest of SAFe, the evidence discipline from Agile SPICE, and the parallel-verification rule from the W-model. Then it adds the two parts none of the six specify well, namely how to slice V-model content into backlog items and how to handle the mismatch between hardware and software cadence.

The overview of that method is in How to Run the V-Model and Agile Sprints at the Same Time. The full version, with a twelve-week worked example on an EV traction inverter, is in the book.

From MBSE Explained

Sprinting through the V

A 43-page field guide to running automotive V-model programmes on real agile sprints — with ASPICE and ISO 26262 evidence produced as you go, not reconstructed before the audit.

Read more about the book →

That's the mission here at MBSE Explained, simplifying systems for smarter EVs. Which of the six is your team running today, and was it a choice?
items.title: V-Model vs Agile in Automotive: Six Hybrid Workflows Compared
items.summary: V-model vs agile is the wrong question in automotive. Six hybrid workflows compared, from Water-Scrum-Fall to SAFe and Agile SPICE, and how to choose one.

items.content_html:
The sprint schedules the work, the V defines the evidence, and the system model is where the two meet.

Almost every automotive programme already runs the V-model and agile sprints at the same time. The V is the process your customer, your quality department and your assessor recognise. The sprint board is where your engineers spend their week. The useful question is how to combine the two so that the sprints shorten feedback loops while the V still produces a defensible engineering record at the end.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. Most advice on this topic stays abstract, and some of it recommends the one arrangement that reliably fails. This post sets out a concrete method instead: what to change, in what order, and what has to stay sequential however agile the team becomes. It is drawn from my field guide, Sprinting through the V.

Can You Use the V-Model and Agile Together?​

Yes, and the standards are not the obstacle. Automotive SPICE defines process outcomes, base practices and work products, and it assesses whether those outcomes are achieved and the evidence exists. It does not mandate a lifecycle. ISO 26262 defines a safety lifecycle, the work products at each level and the confirmation measures around them, and it says nothing about sprint length or how many passes the architecture takes. intacs, the body that certifies ASPICE assessors, even publishes Agile SPICE, a model that maps agile practices onto the assessment so teams can demonstrate compliance in their own working style.

So compatibility is settled. What remains open is the method, and that is where most teams go wrong.

Why Most Teams End Up in Water-Scrum-Fall​

The common move is to introduce Scrum to the development teams and leave everything around them unchanged. Requirements and architecture are still written up front by a different group. Integration and verification still happen at the end. Sprints occupy the middle third of the lifecycle, floating in a sequential process.

Within a few months the pattern is recognisable. Sprint goals turn into activity descriptions such as "continue work on the HV interlock concept". The review has nothing executable to show, so it becomes a status meeting with slides. ASPICE work products are assembled in a documentation push before the assessment, disconnected from the sprints that supposedly produced them. Velocity is measured and never used, because the delivery date was fixed by contract before sprint one.

This is Water-Scrum-Fall, and it is the most common state of the industry. Several popular guides recommend exactly this arrangement under the name of wrapping agile inside the V. It keeps the ceremony overhead of agile and the change resistance of the V, and delivers the benefits of neither, because the feedback loop that actually hurts, from architecture decision to integration result, is as long as it ever was.

What Each Side Gets Right​

Before fixing it, both approaches deserve a fair hearing, because a hybrid that ignores either one gets rejected by the organisation.

The V-model earns its place through three properties. Bidirectional traceability links every requirement to its realisation and its verification, and it is the single most enforced property in an ASPICE assessment. Corresponding verification gives each specification level its own test level, so system requirements are verified by system qualification tests instead of a pile of unit tests. Level discipline keeps register detail out of system requirements and keeps the record navigable. Real forces also push automotive work towards sequence. A PCB spin takes six to ten weeks, a Tier 1 signs against a frozen requirements baseline, and type approval is a one-off event nobody repeats every fortnight.

Agile earns its place through feedback latency. In a strictly sequential V, the gap between making an architectural decision and learning whether it was right can be six to twelve months. By the time integration reveals that the CAN bandwidth budget was optimistic, suppliers have tooled and the safety concept has been written on top of the assumption. Short loops exist to find that out while the decision is still cheap to change.

These two do not conflict. Agile conflicts with the sequential execution of the V, which is a different thing from the V itself.

The Reframe: Evidence and Scheduling​

The way forward is to stop treating the V and the sprint as rival lifecycles competing for the same slot. They answer different questions.

The V-model is a structure of evidence. The sprint is a structure of scheduling. They are orthogonal, and the model is what joins them.

The V answers what artefacts must exist, at what abstraction level, with which trace links, verified by what. It is a static description of a complete, defensible engineering record, and it says nothing about time. Nothing in that structure requires the artefacts to be completed left to right. That ordering is a habit inherited from an era when the artefacts were documents in a filing system.

The sprint answers what gets worked on next, by whom, finished when, and inspected how. It describes flow and says nothing about correctness.

The system model is where they meet. Every backlog item resolves to model elements it creates or changes, and every node in the V's evidence structure is realised by model elements. Two practical rules follow from that. Keep engineering content off the sprint board, so the board tracks work while the model and the requirements tool hold the requirements, architecture and trace links, and each backlog item simply references the model elements it will touch. And treat the sprint increment as a model increment, meaning a larger, still-consistent, more verified model plus whatever it executes: a MiL run, a SiL build, a HIL result, a bench measurement. That is the automotive replacement for "potentially shippable software", and it gives the sprint review something real to inspect.

This only works if the artefacts are model elements. In a document-centric V, a change at the top propagates by hand through a stack of Word files, so iteration genuinely is expensive and the organisation is right to resist it. In a SysML model the change propagates through the model's relationships, which is why MBSE is a precondition for this workflow and why requirements traceability in the model matters so much.

Slice the V Vertically​

This is the step most published hybrid models skip, and the one teams need most.

The intuitive decomposition is by V level, with system requirements in sprint one, architecture in sprint two and software requirements in sprint three. That is horizontal slicing, and it reproduces the sequential V with sprint boundaries drawn on top. Nothing is verified until the layers are stacked, so the feedback latency is unchanged.

A vertical slice is one thin path through the entire V at reduced scope. One capability is specified, architected, allocated, implemented in the model or in code, and verified at the right level, within one or two sprints. For an EV traction inverter, a good first slice is torque command acceptance and limitation under a DC-link voltage constraint. It runs from a stakeholder requirement, through system requirements for torque accuracy and response time, into an allocation to the torque manager block and its interfaces, down to a software requirement and a control model, and it ends with a MiL simulation verified against the response-time requirement. The next slice adds thermal derating, the one after it fault reaction, and then the safety mechanism for unintended torque. Each slice re-traverses the V and deepens the model.

The value lies in what surfaces early. A thin slice drags the interface questions and the abstraction-level disagreements into the open in week two, long before integration in month nine.

The familiar "As a user, I want" story template transfers badly to systems work. This one makes the trace links and the verification method explicit at planning time:

Slice: Torque derating on inverter over-temperature So that: the inverter stays within thermal limits without an abrupt torque loss that would surprise the driver Touching: ThermalManager, TorqueManager, interface IF_ThermalDerate, state machine DeratingStrategy Deriving from: SYS-REQ-0142, SYS-REQ-0143, SG-03 Verified by: MiL simulation of the derating profile against SYS-REQ-0143, with the system qualification test case drafted Safety relevance: ASIL B

Four slicing rules keep it honest:

  • Every story crosses at least two V levels. A story that touches only one level is a task in disguise.
  • Every story ends in a verification artefact, including architecture work, which is verified by review and consistency analysis.
  • The first slices are the ones whose failure would most change the architecture. In a safety-critical domain, value largely means retiring risk early.
  • One story never spans too many levels. A story running from stakeholder requirement to unit test is too big, so split it at the architecture boundary.

Run Three Cadences Instead of One​

A single sprint rhythm cannot carry both a model change and a hardware build. The workflow therefore runs three nested loops, adapted from the nanocycle, microcycle and macrocycle structure in Bruce Powel Douglass's Harmony aMBSE process.

The nanocycle runs from hours to a day. Every model change gets an immediate check, such as re-running the interface consistency check, confirming that a refined requirement is verifiable, or executing a modified state machine against its scenario. No model change is left unchecked overnight. Most of the quality gain comes from this level, and it depends heavily on tooling, because nobody runs a forty-minute manual check every day.

The microcycle is the two-week sprint. It delivers a demonstrable increment built from vertical slices, every completed item meets the Definition of Done including its trace links and verification artefact, and the model is baselined at the sprint boundary. Two weeks suits analysis-heavy systems work better than one week does, and four weeks lets integration debt build up past the point of cheap correction.

The macrocycle is a programme increment of ten to twelve weeks, five or six sprints framed by a planning event and an integration event. This is the layer that faces outward. Customer milestones, A, B and C sample builds, hardware design freezes and gate reviews all attach here, and ten to twelve weeks is also roughly one PCB spin plus assembly and bring-up. The planning event at its start, with systems, software, hardware, test, safety and ideally the supplier in one room, is the single most valuable ceremony in the whole approach. It is SAFe's PI planning event, and it works perfectly well without adopting the rest of SAFe.

Each cadence traverses the V differently:

CadenceHow it traverses the VWhat "done" means
NanocycleOne node, one checkThe change is consistent and executable
MicrocycleOne thin vertical sliceThe slice is specified, allocated, modelled and verified at its level
MacrocycleAll slices integrated across a bandGate criteria met for committed scope, with deferred scope explicit

The V is traversed many times at small scope, and those traversals accumulate into the complete structure. That accumulation is what a gate inspects.

Change the Gate Criteria​

Of everything in this post, this change has the most leverage, and it lives outside engineering.

A traditional gate asks whether the system requirements specification is complete, reviewed and baselined. A sprint delivers slices. After five sprints the team holds a partial specification of high quality, where the gate expected a complete one of unknown quality. If the criterion stays "all artefacts complete across full scope", the documentation push before each gate consumes whatever slack the sprints created, and the programme slides back into Water-Scrum-Fall within two or three cycles.

The fix is to define gates around committed scope: every artefact complete for the scope committed to this milestone, with the remaining scope explicitly deferred and tracked. That decision belongs to programme management and quality. It also explains why so many agile transformations in automotive stall even when the engineering teams do everything right. The part that had to change was never in the engineering department.

What Still Has to Stay Sequential​

A workflow that pretends hardware iterates like software gets rejected by the organisation within two quarters. Some things genuinely cannot run on a two-week loop, including fabricating physical hardware, renegotiating a supplier statement of work, and repeating type approval or an EMC campaign.

The answer is an asymmetry. Iterate at high frequency everything whose cost of change is low (models, requirements, software, simulation), and commit everything whose cost of change is high (hardware builds, supplier scope) at deliberate, well-informed decision points on the macrocycle. Hardware work still happens inside sprints as analysis, tolerance stack-ups, thermal simulation, schematic review and DFMEA sessions. Fabrication is the part that runs on its own cadence. A design freeze then becomes a decision the team takes with evidence in hand, where it used to be a date the programme simply reached.

Safety follows the same logic. Item definition and a first-pass HARA belong in sprint zero, before iteration starts, because they define the boundary inside which iteration is safe. Inside that boundary, safety requirements become backlog items with their own Definition of Done, and the safety case is maintained continuously by a named owner. An architecture change that crosses the boundary triggers a planned impact assessment, which keeps it out of emergency territory.

Questions Teams Ask​

Does Automotive SPICE require the V-model? No. ASPICE defines outcomes and work products and leaves the lifecycle to the organisation. The V in the reference model describes how outputs map to their verification, which is a different thing from a waterfall schedule. If ASPICE compliance is your main concern, see how ASPICE 4.0 aligns with model-based engineering.

Can you iterate a system architecture? Yes, until it has been handed to a supplier with a purchase order attached. That constraint is commercial, and it is an argument for iterating hard before commitment.

What sprint length works for automotive systems teams? Two weeks is the sensible default. It fits analysis-heavy work such as a thermal study or a HARA workshop while keeping integration debt small.

What do you demonstrate at a sprint review without working software? An executed state machine or activity diagram running a scenario, a MiL or SiL simulation showing a control strategy meeting a requirement, a HIL run, a bench measurement, a traceability view from a stakeholder requirement to its verification result, or an analysis result together with its effect on the design. Status slides and "the document is in review" do not count.

Where do the ASPICE work products come from? From the Definition of Done. When every completed item must carry its trace links and its verification artefact, the work products accumulate as a by-product of the sprints, and the assessment no longer needs a four-week reconstruction exercise. The full compliance picture, including what ISO 26262 itself says about agile, is in agile ASPICE and ISO 26262: compliance evidence inside the sprint.

Going Further​

This post covers the core of the method. Choosing between existing frameworks such as SAFe, Agile SPICE and Harmony aMBSE is a separate question, compared in V-Model vs Agile in Automotive: Six Hybrid Workflows Compared. If the V-model itself is new to you, start with the V-model explained.

The full workflow is in the book, including sprint anatomy for a systems team, the three-lane structure for hardware, a twelve-week worked example on an EV traction inverter, Definition of Ready and Done checklists, and a ninety-day adoption roadmap.

Sprinting through the V

Read more about the book →

That's the mission here at MBSE Explained, simplifying systems for smarter EVs. If your team is running sprints inside a V right now, which part breaks first for you: the slicing, the gates, or the hardware cadence?

The XML, the architecture, and now the details behind every block — in one window, with nothing uploaded.

When I first wrote about EasyARXML, the argument was that you shouldn't need an expensive tool licence just to look at an AUTOSAR file someone sent you. Then I rebuilt it to parse entirely in the browser, so the file never leaves your machine.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. Both of those were about getting access to the picture. The picture itself, though, only ever answered one question: what talks to what. Blocks, ports, and the connectors between them.

That's the right question when you open a file cold. It is almost never the question you have thirty seconds later. By then you're pointing at a block asking something more specific — what kind of component is this? What's actually on that port, a Sender-Receiver interface or a Client-Server one with operations? What runs inside it, and how often? Where else is this type used?

Answering any of those meant going back to the XML and resolving path references by hand. So that's what changed. EasyARXML now shows you what's inside the architecture, not just the lines between the boxes — and it does it where the file already is.

If you'd rather watch than read, here's the short version:

Click a Block, See What It Actually Is​

Select any component in the diagram and a panel opens beside it with:

  • What it is — its kind, AUTOSAR path, package and UUID
  • Its ports — each one with its interface and interface kind (Sender-Receiver, Client-Server), and how many connections it has
  • Its runnables — with what triggers each one (Timing · every 100 ms, Operation invoked · Command.SetLock) and which port data it reads or writes
  • Where it's used — for a component type, the places it appears

That last one is quietly useful. "Is this type instantiated anywhere else, and where?" is a question that normally costs you a project-wide search through XML.

Click a Port, Follow the Contract​

Ports get the other half of the picture:

  • The interface contract — its data elements, or for Client-Server, its operations with their arguments and possible errors
  • Every connection on that port — assembly or delegation — and you can click a connection to jump straight to the port on the other end
  • The runnables that use it

That jump is the one I use most. Following a delegation connector by hand means resolving a path reference, scrolling somewhere else entirely, and hoping you kept your place in a file that's thousands of lines long. Now it's a click.

Paths and UUIDs copy to the clipboard with a button, because you're usually about to paste one into a requirements tool or a ticket. The selection survives while you edit the file, clears when you switch to another, and Esc clears it manually.

And It Runs in VS Code​

The second change: EasyARXML is now a VS Code extension, so none of the above requires leaving your editor.

Open any .arxml, run EasyARXML: Open ARXML Preview to the Side from the Command Palette — or click the graph icon in the editor title bar, or right-click the file in the Explorer — and the diagram opens beside the XML. Your cursor stays where it was.

A few things make it usable rather than just a demo:

  • It follows the active editor. Click a different .arxml tab and the diagram switches with it. No re-importing.
  • It re-renders while you type. Edit the XML and the diagram updates live. (There's an easyarxml.liveUpdate setting if you'd rather it didn't.)
  • Fit to view and auto-arrange — the whole architecture on screen in one click. Fit to view deliberately never zooms in past 100%, so a two-component file doesn't fill your screen with giant blocks.
  • It follows your VS Code theme, light or dark.
  • No setup — no configuration, no account, no toolchain.

Still Nothing Leaves Your Machine​

This hasn't changed, and in automotive it's the part that matters most.

The extension reads the file from the open document inside your editor and parses it there. No server, no upload, no account, no telemetry on file contents. It works with your network cable unplugged — which is the easiest possible test, and I'd encourage you to run exactly that one.

You also don't have to take my word for it any more: the extension is MIT licensed, so you or your security team can read precisely what it does before it goes anywhere near a machine with customer ARXML on it.

What It Understands​

Classic AUTOSAR 4.x (the r4.0 schema): application, service and composition software component types as blocks, their P-Ports and R-Ports on those blocks, and both assembly and delegation connectors as the lines between them. Plus, now, the internal behaviour underneath — runnables, their triggering events, and their data access.

It's still a viewer, deliberately. It doesn't edit your ARXML, and it won't replace your configuration tool for the work that genuinely needs one. It removes that tool from the much larger number of moments when all you needed was to look something up.

Getting It​

  • VS Code — EasyARXML on the Marketplace, or search EasyARXML in the Extensions panel
  • Browser — easyarxml.com still works exactly as before, for when someone emails you a file and you just want to glance at it without installing anything

If you work with ARXML daily, get the extension. The browser version is for everyone else who receives one occasionally.

Read more about the book →

items.content_html:
The full chain: SysML for problem and solution domain, UML for the software inside the microcontroller, and generated C++ where it finally becomes code.

Most MBSE presentations end at the same place: a clean architecture diagram, a satisfied nod, and an implicit "…and then the software team implements it." Meanwhile, somewhere down the hall, an embedded developer opens an empty .cpp file and starts typing from scratch — because nothing in that beautiful model told them anything they could actually use.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. That gap is the single biggest credibility problem MBSE has, and it's the one I want to close in this post. I spent nearly five years as a model-based embedded software developer and architect before moving to systems architecture, which means I've stood on both sides of this handoff — and watched it fail from both sides. This is the workflow that actually connects them: SysML for the system, UML for the software, C++ for the target.

Step 1: SysML and the Two Domains​

Before anything becomes code, SysML has one job: separate what the problem is from how you intend to solve it. Collapsing those two is the most common modeling mistake I see, and it poisons everything downstream.

The problem domain describes the system's purpose independently of any solution. Stakeholder needs, operational context, the black-box behavior the vehicle or device must exhibit. In SysML that's use cases, activity diagrams, and requirement diagrams. Crucially, nothing here mentions an ECU, a task, or a class. If you can't describe the problem without naming a microcontroller, you've already jumped to a solution.

The solution domain is where you commit. Logical architecture first — functional blocks and their interfaces, still technology-neutral. Then physical architecture — actual ECUs, sensors, buses, and the allocation of logical functions onto them. This is the same layered progression Capella formalizes in Arcadia, and it's the backbone of the V-model workflow most automotive programs already run.

The output that matters for our purposes is narrow and specific: one bounded chunk of functionality, allocated to one microcontroller, with its interfaces, timing, and safety constraints defined. That allocated slice is the contract. Everything after this point is about realizing it in software.

Step 2: The Handoff Boundary — Where SysML Stops and UML Begins​

This is the part people get wrong, and it's worth slowing down for, because the boundary is a genuine design decision rather than a rule you can look up.

Teams fail in both directions. Some push SysML down into software detail — modeling classes, methods, and data structures in a systems tool. The model becomes enormous, the systems engineers lose the plot, the software engineers won't touch it, and it rots. Others jump straight to UML as soon as an ECU is named, and lose all traceability back to the system requirements that justified the software's existence in the first place.

The division of responsibility that has worked for me:

  • SysML owns what this ECU must do, and why. Allocated requirements, external interfaces, timing and safety constraints, and the traceability back to stakeholder needs.
  • UML owns how the software inside that ECU is structured. Classes, components, state behavior, task decomposition.

The boundary artifact is the software requirement set plus interface specification allocated to that microcontroller. That's the thing that crosses the fence. And the single non-negotiable is that traceability must cross it too — every UML component should trace back to an allocated system requirement. If that chain breaks, you no longer have MBSE; you have two unrelated modeling exercises that happen to be about the same product. That traceability discipline is exactly what I covered in requirements traceability in automotive MBSE.

Step 3: UML Software Architecture Inside the Microcontroller​

Now you're inside the ECU, and the question changes from "what must this do" to "how is this software organized." Four UML views carry most of the weight in embedded work:

  • Class diagrams — the static structure. Components, classes, interfaces, and their relationships. This is the view that will eventually become your C++ headers, so it's worth getting the interfaces honest here.
  • State machine diagrams — the behavior that actually matters in embedded systems. Mode management, startup and shutdown sequences, fault handling and degraded modes. If your device has a "limp home" state, this is where it lives.
  • Sequence diagrams — interaction between components and tasks, especially across asynchronous boundaries. Invaluable for pinning down who calls whom, in what order, and what happens when a message is late.
  • Component and deployment views — mapping software components onto tasks, threads, and scheduling, plus memory and resource allocation.

One practical discipline: model at architecture granularity, not implementation granularity. The moment you start modeling every getter and setter, the model costs more to maintain than the code it describes, and it will be abandoned within two sprints. Model the structure, the interfaces, and the behavior that's hard to reason about in your head. Let the compiler handle the rest.

A note on approach: whether you decompose functionally or object-orientedly genuinely changes what this layer looks like — I dug into that trade-off in functional vs. object-oriented MBSE. For a C++ target, object-oriented decomposition maps more naturally, which is part of why this workflow hangs together.

Step 4: Generating the C++ Skeleton​

Here's where the model finally becomes text you can compile.

StarUML with its C++ extension takes your class diagram and generates C++ skeleton source — headers and implementation stubs with the classes, attributes, operations, and inheritance relationships already in place. You then fill in the behavior.

Be clear-eyed about what that is and isn't. StarUML performs structural generation. It gives you the skeleton; it does not generate behavioral code from your state machines. That distinction matters, because it sets expectations for what the model buys you: consistent structure and interfaces that match the architecture, not a working application.

If you want behavior generated too, that's a different tier of tooling:

  • IBM Engineering Systems Design Rhapsody generates executable code from UML state machines, including full behavioral implementation — the heavyweight option, and genuinely capable.
  • Simulink with Embedded Coder owns the control-algorithm half of the problem: closed-loop control, signal processing, anything continuous. I covered that toolchain in the MathWorks MBSE workflow post.
  • Eclipse Papyrus is the open-source route for UML and SysML together, if licensing is a constraint — one of several options from my open source MBSE tools guide.

A realistic embedded project often uses two of these at once: Simulink-generated control code for the algorithms, and UML-derived structural code for the application and mode-management layers around them.

Step 5: The Second Iteration — The Part Nobody Talks About​

Generating a skeleton once is easy. Every tool demo shows exactly that, and it always looks great.

Then the architecture changes. Meanwhile, the developer has written three hundred lines of real logic into those stubs. Regenerate naively and you destroy their work. Don't regenerate, and the model becomes a historical document that describes a system that no longer exists. This is where model-driven embedded projects actually die — not at generation, but at synchronization.

You get three honest strategies, and you must pick one deliberately:

  1. Generate once, then own the code. The model seeds the project and then becomes documentation. Cheap, and completely fine if you admit that's the deal. The failure mode is pretending the model is still authoritative six months later.
  2. Protected regions. The generator preserves marked blocks of hand-written code across regenerations. This works, and it's the common middle ground — but the markers are brittle, merges get unpleasant, and refactoring across the boundary is painful.
  3. Full generation. The model is the single source of truth and code is a build artifact nobody edits by hand. The highest discipline and the highest payoff — architecture changes propagate automatically — but it demands mature tooling (Rhapsody-class) and a team genuinely willing to stop editing generated files.

Whichever you choose, enforce it in CI. Regenerate from the model in the pipeline and fail the build on unexpected diffs. A sync strategy that lives only in a wiki page is a sync strategy that has already failed.

The Automotive Reality Check​

Three constraints that will shape this workflow in a real program:

MISRA C++ compliance. Generated code is still code, and it still has to pass your coding standard. Generators are not automatically MISRA-clean — check what your generator emits before you commit to it, not during your first static-analysis run.

ISO 26262 tool qualification. If generated code ends up in a safety-relevant path, your code generator becomes a tool requiring confidence assessment and potentially qualification. That's a real cost, and it's a strong argument for using a qualified commercial generator rather than a community extension on anything ASIL-rated.

Where C++ actually fits. Classic AUTOSAR is a C world — this workflow is not aimed there. It fits Adaptive AUTOSAR (C++14 and later), higher-compute ECUs, and non-AUTOSAR embedded products like ODM IoT hardware, where you control the whole stack. Being honest about that boundary is better than promising a workflow that won't survive contact with a Classic ECU.

What Good Looks Like​

Pulling the chain together: stakeholder needs and black-box behavior in SysML's problem domain; logical then physical architecture in the solution domain, ending with functionality allocated to a specific microcontroller; a clean handoff artifact of software requirements plus interfaces, with traceability crossing the boundary; UML class, state, sequence, and deployment views at architecture granularity inside the ECU; C++ skeletons generated from the structural model; and a consciously chosen, CI-enforced synchronization strategy holding it all together over time.

None of this requires a heroic toolchain. It requires deciding where each model's authority begins and ends — and then being disciplined enough not to blur those lines when a deadline arrives.

That's the mission here at MBSE Explained — simplifying systems for smarter EVs. Where does this chain break in your organization: the SysML-to-UML handoff, or keeping the model and the code in sync afterwards? I'd genuinely like to know in the comments — it's the question I get asked most.
items.title: From SysML to C++ - The MBSE Workflow from System Model to Embedded Code
items.summary: A practical MBSE workflow from SysML problem and solution domain, through UML software architecture inside the microcontroller, to generated C++ skeletons and embedded code - including the round-trip problem nobody talks about.

items.content_html:
Two updates to EasyARXML: the parser now runs entirely in your browser, and you can export the diagram as a PDF report.

A while back I wrote about why reading an ARXML file shouldn't cost you a tool license, and introduced EasyARXML — a free, in-browser viewer that turns an AUTOSAR .arxml into a diagram of software components, ports and connectors. Since then I've made two changes that matter enough to write about, because both came directly from the same realization: I was building for automotive engineers, and the first version didn't fully respect what that means.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. This is a short, honest changelog — what changed, and why.

1. It No Longer Touches a Server​

The first version of EasyARXML parsed ARXML server-side. You'd drop a file, it would go up to a backend, get parsed, and the diagram would come back. Technically fine. Architecturally wrong — for this audience specifically.

Here's the problem I should have led with from day one: ARXML describes confidential vehicle software. It's covered by NDAs, it's competitively sensitive, and nobody in automotive should be uploading it to a random web tool — mine included. A viewer that quietly ships your file to a server it doesn't control is asking you to do exactly the thing your security and legal teams tell you not to do. The convenience isn't worth it, and honestly it shouldn't have been on the table.

So the parser moved into the browser. Now your file is read locally, rendered locally, and never leaves your machine. There's no upload, no server round-trip, no storage. And you don't have to take my word for it — open your browser's Network tab, drop in a file, and watch. It takes about five seconds to confirm that nothing goes out. That verifiability is the point: privacy you can check beats privacy you're asked to trust.

This one change is what makes EasyARXML usable inside an automotive organization at all. Everything else is a feature. This is the foundation.

2. Download a PDF Report​

The second change is about getting the diagram out of the browser and into your workflow.

You can now auto-arrange the diagram and export it as a PDF — software components, ports and connectors, laid out cleanly on a page. It's something you can actually attach to a review, drop into a design discussion, or hand to an integrator who needs to see the structure without opening any tooling at all.

That closes a small but real gap. Viewing an ARXML in your browser is useful; being able to share what you saw — as a clean artifact, not a screenshot — is what makes it part of a real review loop instead of a throwaway glance.

Why This Exists At All​

Both changes trace back to the same everyday annoyance that made me build EasyARXML in the first place. I kept opening heavyweight configuration tools — the kind that take real time just to launch — for one small question: "what actually changed in this file?" Or an even simpler one: "what's in this thing a supplier just sent me?"

That's not a job that should require a full authoring seat, a license checkout, or a wait on a shared license pool. It's a reading task. And reading tasks are frequent, quick, and — done right — should be private and free. EasyARXML is my attempt to make that specific moment painless: open the file, see the architecture, export it if you need to, and never once worry about where the file went.

It's a viewer, deliberately — it doesn't replace your configurator for the work that genuinely needs one. It just removes that tool from the large number of moments when all you needed was to look.

If you work with ARXML, try it with one of your own files — and if you still don't trust it, that's exactly what the Network tab is for.

That's the mission here at MBSE Explained — simplifying systems for smarter EVs. What's the ARXML task that most often makes you reach for a heavyweight tool when you wish you didn't have to? Tell me in the comments — it shapes what I build next.
items.title: EasyARXML Rebuilt - It No Longer Touches a Server and exports PDF report
items.summary: Two changes that matter for automotive teams: EasyARXML now parses ARXML entirely in your browser (your file never leaves your machine) and can export the diagram as a shareable PDF report.

items.content_html:
What an ARXML file actually contains: software components, their ports, and the connectors between them — shown here as a diagram instead of raw XML.

If you've worked anywhere near automotive embedded software, you've had this moment: a colleague or a supplier sends you a file ending in .arxml, and you open it expecting something readable — and get a wall of angle-bracketed XML thousands of lines deep, describing what appears to be three software components and a couple of ports. Somewhere in there is the information you actually need. Good luck finding it by eye.

Welcome to MBSE Explained. ARXML is one of those formats that's absolutely central to modern vehicle software and yet rarely explained in plain terms — most engineers meet it through a tool, never quite sure what the file underneath is. This post fixes that: what ARXML actually is, what it describes, where it sits in the AUTOSAR workflow, and why the raw file is so punishing to read. In the next post I'll get into the more pointed problem — what it costs just to look at one — but you need the format itself first.

What ARXML Actually Is​

ARXML stands for AUTOSAR XML. AUTOSAR — AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture — is the standard that a large chunk of the industry uses to structure automotive software, so that a braking-controller component from one supplier and an OEM's platform software can be designed against the same rules and actually fit together.

ARXML is the file format AUTOSAR defines to describe that software. It's plain XML, but constrained by an AUTOSAR schema, so every element means something specific and standardized. Crucially, ARXML isn't the code that runs on the ECU — it's the formal description of the architecture: what the software components are, what data they exchange, how they connect, and how they map onto hardware. Think of it as the machine-readable blueprint that the code is generated against and configured from.

The reason the format exists at all is exchange. Automotive programs are built by many companies using many different tools — OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, tool vendors — and none of them want to be locked into a single toolchain. A standardized, tool-agnostic file format means an architecture defined in one tool can be handed to another party and read in theirs. ARXML is that interchange contract.

What's Inside an ARXML File​

Strip away the XML verbosity and an ARXML file is describing a handful of core concepts. For Classic AUTOSAR — the platform running on the deeply embedded ECUs in a vehicle — the ones you meet most often are:

  • Software Components (SWCs) — the building blocks of the application. A SensorSWC, a ControllerSWC, an ActuatorSWC. Each is a self-contained unit of behavior.
  • Ports — how a component talks to the outside world. A P-Port (provider) offers data or a service; an R-Port (requirer) consumes it. This provider/requirer split is the heart of how AUTOSAR components stay decoupled.
  • Interfaces — the contract on a port: what data elements or operations flow through it. Two components only connect cleanly if their ports share a compatible interface.
  • Compositions — a way to group components into a larger component, so the architecture can be nested rather than flat. A composition has its own ports and holds other components inside it.
  • Connectors — the actual wiring. Assembly connectors join one component's P-Port to another's R-Port; delegation connectors pass a composition's internal port out to its boundary.

On top of that structural picture, ARXML also carries the ECU configuration (how the standardized basic-software modules are parameterized for a specific ECU) and system description information (how components map onto ECUs and onto the communication buses between them). A file called an ECU extract is exactly what it sounds like — the slice of the whole system description relevant to one ECU.

You don't need to hold all of that in your head. The point is that ARXML spans a spectrum: at one end, a clean architectural view of components and how they're wired; at the other, dense low-level configuration. A given file might be mostly one or mostly the other.

Where ARXML Sits in the Workflow​

ARXML isn't a thing you sit down and write. It's generated and consumed at several points along the AUTOSAR development flow, roughly like this:

  1. System and software architecture is defined — increasingly in an MBSE or dedicated AUTOSAR authoring tool — producing ARXML that describes the components, their ports, and their interfaces.
  2. That ARXML is exchanged between parties. An OEM hands an ECU extract to a Tier 1; a Tier 1 hands component descriptions back. This is where the format's standardization earns its keep.
  3. The descriptions drive RTE and basic-software configuration — the AUTOSAR Runtime Environment that actually glues components to each other and to the ECU is generated from what the ARXML specifies.
  4. Throughout, ARXML gets reviewed, integrated, and diffed as the architecture evolves — which is where a lot of day-to-day engineering time actually goes.

So ARXML is simultaneously an authoring output, an interchange format, a configuration source, and a review artifact. That's a lot of jobs for one file type, and it's why ARXML files end up everywhere in an automotive software program.

Why the Raw File Is So Hard to Read​

Here's the honest tension at the center of ARXML: it's designed to be machine-readable and unambiguous, which is the right call for a format that tools generate and consume — and that same design makes it miserable for a human to read directly.

A trivial architecture — three components, a few ports, a connector or two — can run to thousands of lines of nested XML, with references between elements expressed as long path-like strings rather than anything you can follow visually. The information is all there, precisely. It's just not shaped for a person. Nobody looks at raw ARXML and immediately sees "ah, SensorSWC's output feeds ControllerSWC, which drives ActuatorSWC." You see that in a diagram. In the XML, that same fact is scattered across component definitions, port definitions, interface definitions, and connector definitions, tied together by references you have to resolve in your head.

That gap — between what the file contains and what a human can see — is the whole reason tooling exists around ARXML. The banner on this post is exactly that translation: the same components, ports, and connectors an ARXML describes, rendered as a graph you can actually read at a glance.

Pulling It Together​

ARXML is the standardized XML format AUTOSAR uses to describe automotive software architecture — components, ports, interfaces, connectors, and ECU configuration — and it exists so that a fragmented, multi-vendor toolchain can exchange that architecture without lock-in. It's central, it's precise, and in raw form it's almost unreadable by design, which is why nobody actually works with it as text if they can help it.

That sets up the more uncomfortable question I want to tackle next: given that you constantly need to read these files — to review a supplier's work, to understand something a colleague sent, to sanity-check an integration — why is simply opening one so often gated behind an expensive tool license? That's the subject of the next post.

That's the mission here at MBSE Explained — simplifying systems for smarter EVs. If ARXML has ever ruined an afternoon for you, tell me how in the comments — I'd like to hear which part of the format trips your team up most.
items.title: ARXML Explained: What AUTOSAR's XML Format Really Is, and the Workflow Around It
items.summary: A plain-English guide to ARXML - what the AUTOSAR XML format describes, where it sits in the automotive software workflow, and why the raw file is so hard to read.

items.content_html:
Drop an ARXML file into EasyARXML and see its components, ports and connectors instantly — free, in the browser, with nothing uploaded.

In the last post I walked through what ARXML actually is: the standardized, precise, and — in raw form — nearly unreadable XML that describes AUTOSAR software architecture. I ended on a question, and this post is the answer to it. Given that reading these files is a constant, unavoidable part of automotive software work, why is opening one so often gated behind a license you have to fight for?

Welcome to MBSE Explained. This one is personal, because it's the exact annoyance that made me build a tool to fix it. Let me lay out the problem first, because if you've lived it you'll recognize every step.

The Everyday Absurdity​

Here's the scene. A supplier sends over an ECU extract for review. Or a colleague on another team asks you to sanity-check the component structure in an ARXML they've been working on. You don't need to edit anything. You don't need to generate an RTE. You just need to look — to see which components are there, how the ports connect, whether the architecture matches what was agreed.

So you go to open it, and one of a few things happens. You fire up a heavyweight AUTOSAR authoring or configuration tool — the kind that takes real time just to load — to perform what amounts to a five-minute read. Or you go to check out a license from the shared pool and find every seat is taken, so you wait, or you ping the person hoarding one. Or you don't have a license assigned to you at all, because you're an integrator, a reviewer, or a manager who only occasionally needs to see an ARXML, and nobody budgeted a full authoring seat for that.

Either way, a read-only task just consumed a scarce, expensive resource — or stalled entirely waiting for one.

Why This Happens​

None of this is anyone being unreasonable. It's structural. The tools that author and configure ARXML — the DaVinci-style developer and configurator tools, the tresos-style configuration environments, and their peers — are genuinely powerful, genuinely necessary for the work they're built for, and priced accordingly. Organizations buy a limited number of floating licenses and share them across a team, because per-seat licensing at those prices doesn't scale to "everyone who might ever need to look."

The result is a license pool sized for the people doing authoring work — and everyone else who merely needs to read an ARXML is quietly drawing from that same small pool. Reviewers, integrators, test engineers, architects doing a quick cross-check, managers verifying a deliverable: all of them, to answer a simple "what's in this file," are told to occupy a seat built for someone doing eight hours of configuration.

It's a mismatch between the tool's cost model and the most common actual use case. Reading is frequent, quick, and low-stakes. Authoring is rarer, longer, and expensive. Charging both at the authoring rate is where the friction lives.

And You Can't Just Use a Web Tool​

The obvious modern instinct is "surely there's a website where I can just drop the file in." And for most file formats, there would be. For ARXML, there's a hard blocker: confidentiality.

An ARXML file describes real vehicle software architecture. It's covered by NDAs, it's competitively sensitive, and in many organizations it is flatly against policy to upload it to some random online converter that ships your file off to a server you know nothing about. So the one thing that would make quick reads easy — a browser tool — is exactly the thing security and legal won't let you touch, because the typical web tool means handing your confidential file to someone else's backend. That concern is completely valid, and it's why "just use an online viewer" has historically been a non-starter in automotive.

What I Built Instead: EasyARXML​

This is the problem EasyARXML exists to solve, and I built it around that confidentiality constraint rather than ignoring it.

EasyARXML is a free, in-browser viewer for AUTOSAR ARXML files. You open easyarxml.com, drop in a .arxml, and it renders the architecture — software components, their P-Ports and R-Ports, compositions, and the assembly and delegation connectors between them — as an interactive diagram you can pan, auto-arrange, and read at a glance. The banner on this post is that output on a real file.

The part that makes it usable in automotive specifically: the file never leaves your machine. EasyARXML parses the ARXML entirely in your browser with JavaScript — there's no upload, no server round-trip, no storage, no telemetry on your file. You don't have to take my word for it, either: open your browser's Network tab while you load a file and watch for yourself. Nothing goes out. That's the whole point — it answers the NDA objection at the architecture level, not with a promise but with the absence of an upload.

Beyond that, it's deliberately simple:

  • Free — no sign-up, no account, no trial wall. Open a file and go.
  • Nothing to install — runs in any modern browser on Windows, macOS, or Linux, and works offline once the page has loaded.
  • Fast — you skip loading a heavyweight toolchain just to understand a file someone sent you.
  • Export to PDF — auto-arrange the diagram and download a clean report to share or archive.

It reads Classic AUTOSAR 4.x files, and it is honestly scoped: EasyARXML is a viewer, not an authoring tool. It doesn't replace your configurator for the work that genuinely needs one — it removes that tool from the huge number of moments when all you needed was to look. Free up the expensive seats for the people actually authoring, and let everyone else read for free.

Pulling It Together​

The ARXML license trap is a mismatch: reading these files is constant and cheap in effort, but the tools that open them are priced and licensed for authoring. Add a legitimate confidentiality constraint that rules out ordinary web tools, and you get a genuinely annoying gap — one where people burn expensive seats, or wait on a pool, to do something that should take fifteen seconds.

EasyARXML is my answer to that gap: open any ARXML as a diagram, free, in your browser, with your file never leaving your computer. If you've ever queued for a license just to review someone's work, try it with one of your own files and tell me how it goes.

That's the mission here at MBSE Explained — simplifying systems for smarter EVs. How does your team handle ARXML reviews today — shared license pool, or something better? I'd genuinely like to know in the comments.
